drills.title: Half-life from a quarterly AR(1)
drills.question: A cap-rate spread follows a quarterly AR(1) with phi = 0.85. (a) What is the half-life in quarters? (b) What is the equivalent annual persistence coefficient?
drills.solution: H = ln 0.5 / ln 0.85 = -0.6931 / -0.1625 = 4.27 quarters (about 1.07 years). Annual persistence = 0.85^4 = 0.522.
common_mistakes: Reporting 4.27 years: the half-life is in the period of the data (quarters)
Using 4 x 0.85 or 0.85/4 for the annual coefficient instead of 0.85^4
drills.intuition: Each quarter keeps 85% of the deviation; it takes a little over four quarters to lose half.
drills.takeaway: Always state the period of phi; estimated phi near one is biased down, so the true half-life is probably longer.

drills.title: One likelihood-ratio update
drills.question: Your prior that a lender will pull back from hotel lending this year is 25%. A loan officer's comment is 2.4 times as likely if the pullback is coming. What is your posterior probability (%)?
drills.solution: Prior odds = 0.25/0.75 = 1/3. Posterior odds = 1/3 x 2.4 = 0.8. Posterior = 0.8/1.8 = 44.4%.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the probability by the LR (25% x 2.4 = 60%)
Ignoring that an anecdote's LR is itself uncertain
drills.intuition: Likelihood ratios multiply odds, not probabilities.
drills.takeaway: Convert to odds, multiply, convert back. Record the LR before you see the outcome.

drills.title: Loop gain up and down
drills.question: Pledged collateral in a market is $200bn, lenders advance 65%, owners draw half of new capacity, and each $1bn of net demand moves prices 0.8%. (a) Loop gain on the way up. (b) Multiplier. (c) Total price rise (%) from a +3% fundamental shock. (d) The downside multiplier if 90% of collateral must repay lost capacity. (e) What does the gap between (b) and (d) imply for leverage decisions?

rubric: States that borrowing is optional but repayment is forced, so downside gain exceeds upside gain
Notes the downside gain 0.936 is near the stability boundary and the linear model is only a fragility indicator
Concludes leverage should be sized to the downside loop, not the upside one
Mentions that lenders cutting LTV after losses would raise the downside gain further

drills.solution: m_up = 0.65 x 0.5 x 200 x 0.008 = 0.52; multiplier 1/0.48 = 2.08; total 3% x 2.083 = 6.25%. m_down = 0.65 x 0.9 x 200 x 0.008 = 0.936; multiplier 1/0.064 = 15.6. The same market is mildly amplifying up and close to unstable down.
common_mistakes: Using the same theta in both directions
Treating 15.6x as a forecast rather than a fragility signal
drills.intuition: Owners choose how much new capacity to use; borrowers at the covenant limit have no choice about repaying.
drills.takeaway: Stress tests should use the downside loop gain.

drills.title: Build now or wait
drills.question: A completed building would be worth $20.0m today and $24.0m or $17.0m next year. Construction costs $18.5m now or 3% more next year. The completed building yields 5% cash on today's value; the risk-free rate is 4%. (a) Static NPV ($m). (b) Risk-neutral probability. (c) Value of waiting ($m). (d) Build or wait, and what would change the answer?

rubric: Chooses to wait because 1.90 > 1.50, and calls the 0.40 difference the option premium
Names the costs of waiting: forgone yield, cost inflation, entitlement or competitive pre-emption risk
States that lower uncertainty or higher yield would favor building now
Notes that land priced at residual (1.5) undervalues the option

common_mistakes: Discounting at the real-world probability without adjusting for risk
Forgetting the forgone 5% yield or the cost escalation
drills.intuition: Waiting lets you skip the bad state; you pay for that with the yield and cost inflation you forgo.
drills.takeaway: Positive NPV is necessary but not sufficient to build now.

drills.title: Margin call with price impact
drills.question: A fund holds 200 units, now priced at 47, with debt of 7,200 and a 75% LTV covenant. (a) Units to sell with no price impact. (b) Units to sell if each unit sold lowers the price by 0.02 (all units marked at the post-sale price). (c) Post-sale price. (d) Remaining equity. (e) Is the fund near the spiral zone?

rubric: Computes the marginal threshold (1-0.75) x 47/(0.75 x 200) = 0.078 and compares it with 0.02
Notes impact raised the forced sale by about a third
Recognizes that other holders of the same asset now face lower marks
Says the cure is feasible but the buffer should have been sized to include impact

common_mistakes: Selling just enough to repay the dollar excess (debt - 0.75 x value) instead of dividing by 1 - 0.75
Ignoring the mark-down on retained units
drills.intuition: Each dollar sold repays a dollar of debt but lowers allowed debt by 75 cents, and impact lowers the value of everything you keep.
drills.takeaway: Covenant buffers must include your own price impact.

drills.title: Exit capacity alone and crowded
drills.question: You hold $30m of a REIT that trades $12m a day; you will not exceed 10% of volume. Similar funds hold $180m in total including yours. (a) Days to exit alone. (b) Days for the crowd to exit together.
drills.solution: Alone: 30/(0.10 x 12) = 25 days. Crowd: 180/1.2 = 150 days, which is also your exit time if capacity is shared pro rata.
common_mistakes: Using total ADV rather than the participation share
Assuming your exit is unaffected by others' selling
drills.intuition: In a stress, exit capacity is shared with everyone who must sell.
drills.takeaway: Size to crowded exit time relative to your funding horizon.

drills.title: The broker's two-year downturn
drills.question: Your quarterly regime model, fitted on two decades of hotel data with three contractions, gives p22 = 0.85. A broker says 'hotel downturns last two years on average, so a six-quarter bridge loan gets you through'. A contraction has just begun. (a) Model-implied expected duration (quarters). (b) Probability the contraction lasts more than 8 quarters. (c) Probability it is still under way after the loan's 6 quarters. (d) Reconcile the model with the broker and decide whether the bridge loan is acceptable.

rubric: Notes the model's mean (1.67 years) and the broker's (2 years) differ, and that with three contractions neither is precise
Points out that even if the broker's average were right, the duration distribution is wide: averages do not get you through
Uses the 38% probability of maturing inside the contraction as the key risk number
Considers extension options, interest reserves, or a longer loan
Flags the geometric (memoryless) assumption as itself questionable

drills.solution: E[D] = 1/(1-0.85) = 6.67 quarters. P(D > 8) = 0.85^8 = 0.272. P(still in contraction after 6 quarters) = 0.85^6 = 0.377. A loan whose term equals the average duration matures inside the contraction more than a third of the time under the model.
common_mistakes: Matching loan term to the average duration
Treating the broker's claim and the model as independent confirmations
Trusting p22 estimated from three episodes to two decimals
drills.intuition: Durations are skewed: many short downturns and a few long ones. The long ones are the ones that hurt.
drills.takeaway: Size debt maturities to the tail of the duration distribution, not its mean.

drills.title: Three signals, unknown dependence: bid or abstain
drills.question: A seller wants a firm bid in five days on a hotel worth about $19m if the market holds and $15m in a downturn; the ask is $17.5m. Your prior on a downturn is 30%. In the past week: one month of RevPAR -3%, a competing hotel announcement, and a broker telling you buyers are 'everywhere'. You cannot estimate likelihood ratios with any confidence, and the first two signals may reflect the same supply event. What do you do?

rubric: Computes the break-even downturn probability: 19 - 4p = 17.5 gives p = 0.375, before any margin of safety
Recognizes the prior (0.30) is already close to break-even, so the decision depends on LRs that cannot be estimated
Identifies the dependence between RevPAR and the supply announcement and the low information content of the broker's comment
Concludes that abstaining or bidding only with a price well below ask (with a margin of safety) is the disciplined answer given a five-day deadline
Names the data that would resolve it (STR supply pipeline, group pace, three months of RevPAR) and says the seller's deadline is itself information

drills.solution: Expected value at the prior is 19 - 4 x 0.30 = 17.8, only 1.7% above ask. Break-even p = 0.375. Any reasonable LR for the RevPAR print (say 2) would push the posterior above break-even (odds 0.429 x 2 = 0.857, p = 0.46), while an LR near 1 would leave it below. With dependent signals and a five-day deadline you cannot tell which. The best answer is to abstain, or to bid only at a price that works at a posterior of about 0.5 (19 - 2 = 17.0, less a margin), and to walk away if refused.
common_mistakes: Inventing precise LRs to force a decision
Counting the RevPAR print and the supply announcement as independent evidence
Treating the broker's enthusiasm as evidence about fundamentals
drills.intuition: When the decision hinges on numbers you cannot estimate, the value of waiting for information exceeds the value of the deal.
drills.takeaway: Abstention is a position. Take it when the prior is near break-even and the evidence is unweighable.
